big_story.text: Paramount closed its $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery on Tuesday, a day after Justice Kagan refused a last-minute bid to block it, creating the media giant Skydance — while the S&P 500 hit its first record close since August.

stories.headline: Paramount closes $110B Warner Bros. takeover after Supreme Court refuses to block it

whos_who.name: Paramount
whos_who.description: US film/TV group run by David Ellison

whos_who.name: Warner Bros. Discovery
whos_who.description: owner of Warner studios, HBO Max, CNN

whos_who.name: Skydance
whos_who.description: new name of the combined company

whos_who.name: Elena Kagan
whos_who.description: Supreme Court justice handling 9th Circuit emergencies

stories.body: On Monday Justice Kagan denied, without explanation, an emergency application from consumers who wanted the merger halted; lower courts and the 9th Circuit had already rejected them. The deal closed Tuesday, with Warner shareholders receiving about $31 per share in cash. To settle suits by 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild, Paramount promised 30 films a year for two years, to keep both Los Angeles studio lots for five years, and an editorial board to protect CNN's and CBS News' independence.
stories.why_it_matters: It ends one of the biggest merger fights of the year with no federal challenge, and puts CNN, CBS News, HBO Max and Paramount+ under one owner targeting about $6B in cost savings — which likely means job cuts.
plain_words: Two of Hollywood's biggest companies are now one.
Some customers tried at the last minute to get the highest court to stop it, but it said no.
The new company owns Harry Potter, CNN and many TV channels, and plans to save money, probably by cutting jobs.

stories.headline: Supreme Court appears ready to side with Intel against workers in 401(k) investment suit

whos_who.name: ERISA
whos_who.description: federal law protecting worker retirement plans

whos_who.name: 9th Circuit
whos_who.description: federal appeals court for the western US

stories.body: At Tuesday's argument in *Anderson v. Intel*, a majority of justices signalled that workers who say their plan's investments underperformed must point to a "meaningful benchmark" *(a comparable fund with similar goals and risks)*. Intel's plan put up to about 37% of one fund into hedge funds, private equity and commodities after 2008; the 9th Circuit threw out the suit because the workers compared it with ordinary stock-heavy funds. Justice Kagan said a benchmark must be "meaningfully similar — that doesn't mean identical," while others questioned how detailed the Court's guidance should be.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling will set how easily employees can sue over retirement-plan choices; a tough benchmark rule would end many lawsuits early and make it safer for plans to add private-equity and other alternative investments.
plain_words: Intel workers say the company put their retirement money into risky, expensive investments that did badly.
The judges seemed to think you can only call an investment bad if you compare it with something truly similar.
That would make it harder for workers to win cases like this.

stories.headline: Groq investors sue its former board in Delaware over Nvidia's $20B "reverse acqui-hire"

whos_who.name: Groq
whos_who.description: US maker of AI inference chips

stories.body: Two former Groq engineers and shareholders filed a proposed class action, unsealed on Monday, accusing Groq's board and Ross of breaching their fiduciary duties *(the legal duty to act in all shareholders' best interest)*. In December 2025 Nvidia paid about $20B to license Groq's technology and hire Ross and around 200 engineers — a "reverse acqui-hire" *(buying a startup's people and tech without buying the company itself)*. The plaintiffs say the structure skipped a shareholder vote and left remaining investors with a weakened shell; Nvidia is not a defendant and Groq calls the suit meritless.
stories.why_it_matters: Big Tech has used this deal structure to grab AI talent while avoiding merger reviews; a Delaware ruling could decide whether boards owe ordinary shareholders the same protections as in a normal takeover.
plain_words: Nvidia took Groq's best ideas and engineers without officially buying the company.
Some Groq shareholders say the bosses got rich while they were left with a weaker business.
They want a judge to make it right.

stories.headline: Texas court applies Texas law to past Coinbase conduct and throws out shareholder suit

whos_who.name: Texas Business Court
whos_who.description: new Texas court for company disputes

whos_who.name: Delaware
whos_who.description: state where most big US companies are incorporated

stories.body: Judge Andrea Bouressa dismissed a derivative suit *(a case shareholders bring on the company's behalf against its own managers)* against Coinbase executives on Monday. She ruled that Texas law governs because Coinbase moved its incorporation from Delaware to Texas in December 2025 — even for conduct from before the move — calling it a bright-line rule that brings "clarity and certainty."
stories.why_it_matters: It is an early test of whether leaving Delaware for Texas, whose 2025 reforms make shareholder suits harder, also shields managers from claims about the past; that could push more companies to reincorporate.
plain_words: Coinbase moved its legal home from Delaware to Texas, where the rules are friendlier to company bosses.
A Texas judge said the Texas rules apply even to things that happened before the move.
So the shareholders' case against the bosses was thrown out.

stories.headline: S&P 500 tops 7,800 for first record close since August as Treasury yields retreat

whos_who.name: Nvidia
whos_who.description: AI chipmaker, world's most valuable company

stories.body: The S&P 500 rose 0.58% to 7,818.93 and the Nasdaq 0.45% to a record 27,599.79, led by tech as Nvidia closed in on a $6 trillion market value and AMD gained 2.8%. The 10-year Treasury yield eased 3.6 basis points to 5.275% after Monday's 24-year high, and Brent fell 1.6% to $98.67 as a G7 oil-reserve release eased supply worries. Small caps lagged, with the Russell 2000 down 0.59%.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia, Apple and Microsoft now make up over 21% of the S&P 500, a record concentration, so the index depends heavily on a few AI winners; the Fed's meeting minutes due Wednesday are the next test for yields.
plain_words: The main US stock index reached its highest level ever.
Big tech companies, especially AI chip makers, did most of the work.
Interest rates on government loans dipped a little, which helped.

stories.headline: Google signs 3.6-gigawatt power deal with Constellation Energy; its shares jump 12%

whos_who.name: Google
whos_who.description: search and cloud giant, unit of Alphabet

stories.body: Google agreed a 20-year power purchase agreement *(a long-term contract to buy electricity at set terms)* for 890 MW of new nuclear output, which Constellation will create by investing over $4.3B to upgrade 11 reactors in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey, with first gains due by 2028. A separate 15-year deal covers another 2,700 MW from Constellation's fleet. Constellation shares rose about 12% and other nuclear stocks such as Oklo and NuScale rallied.
stories.why_it_matters: AI data centres are driving a race for reliable power; PJM expects peak demand to rise by up to 30 GW by 2030, and tech giants are now paying to expand existing nuclear plants.
plain_words: AI computers need huge amounts of electricity.
Google promised to buy power from a nuclear company for 20 years, and that company will upgrade its plants to make more.
Investors loved it and pushed the share price up.

stories.headline: McKesson and CD&R agree $5.8B take-private of home-infusion firm Option Care Health
stories.body: The buyers will pay $32.05 per share in cash, a 37.1% premium, valuing the company at about $5.8B including debt; Option Care shares jumped about 33%. CD&R takes a majority stake while McKesson invests $1.4B for 49%, with an option to buy the rest later. Option Care gives patients infusions *(medicine through a drip into a vein)* at home or in small clinics, more than 300,000 a year, and closing is expected in the first half of 2027.
stories.why_it_matters: It moves McKesson deeper into care delivered at home rather than in hospitals, a cheaper setting that an ageing population is making more important.
plain_words: A big medicine wholesaler and an investment firm are buying a company that gives patients drip treatments at home.
They are paying much more than the share price, so its shareholders gained a lot in one day.
More medical care is moving from hospitals to people's homes.

stories.headline: UBS hands ex-Credit Suisse fund administration to Northern Trust; SMI gains 0.6%

whos_who.name: Credit Suisse
whos_who.description: rival bank UBS took over in 2023

whos_who.name: SMI
whos_who.description: index of the 20 biggest Swiss companies

stories.body: UBS will exit fund administration *(the back-office work of valuing funds and keeping their books)* in Switzerland and Luxembourg, moving the former Credit Suisse businesses to Northern Trust from the second quarter of 2027, with a two-year migration; terms were not disclosed. UBS shares rose 1.4%. The SMI closed up 0.62% at 13,788.93, led by Amrize (+1.7%) and Holcim (+1.4%), though pharma stocks gave up early gains in the afternoon; USD/CHF ended near 0.8308, little changed.
stories.why_it_matters: It is another step in UBS shrinking the Credit Suisse legacy to cut costs and focus on its core businesses such as wealth management.
plain_words: UBS is handing a boring but necessary bookkeeping job to an American bank that does it at bigger scale.
That saves UBS money and effort.
Swiss shares rose a bit on the day.

stories.headline: Mistral launches Large 4, a 1-trillion-parameter model trained in its own European data centres

whos_who.name: Mistral
whos_who.description: French AI startup, Europe's leading model maker

stories.body: The natively multimodal model (49B active parameters) is in public preview now, with open weights due by the end of October; Mistral trained it on about 3,800 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs and prices it at $1.36 per million input tokens.
plain_words: A French company released a very large AI model that can read text and images.
It built and trained it in Europe, without relying on US cloud giants.
Soon anyone will be able to download and run it.

stories.headline: Meta and Sierra propose open standard for personal AI agents to deal with businesses

whos_who.name: Sierra
whos_who.description: US startup building customer-service AI agents

stories.body: The "Personal Agent Protocol" sets rules for how a user's AI assistant logs in to a company, what data it may use and what it is allowed to do; the full spec and reference code are due by the end of October.
plain_words: Soon your AI assistant might shop or book things for you.
This is a shared set of rules so it can talk safely to stores and companies.
Each company decides what the assistant may do, and you control your data.
